As of 223 AM EDT Saturday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Patchy morning frost across the northwestern Adirondacks 
and Essex County, Vermont remains on track where the combination of 
temperatures in the low to mid 30s and light winds around daybreak 
are most likely. Otherwise, uneventful weather is expected today 
while weak upper level ridging glides across our region concurrent 
with surface high pressure. The ridge axis kicks to our east tonight 
in advance of a shortwave trough and wave of low pressure 
approaching from our west. This system will bring our anticipated 
rain event for Sunday. The majority of model guidance favors 
steadier rain, and greater rainfall amounts, in our southern areas. 
However, a cluster of models has more uniform rain areawide/farther 
north, possibly associated with stronger 850 millibar warm air 
advection while a closed low tracks over the eastern Great Lakes, as 
opposed to an open wave. 

In any event, increasing confidence and statistical likelihood 
of steady rain during much of the daylight hours has led to 
lowering of temperatures with temperatures quite cool. In fact, 
forecast highs in the low to mid 50s are near or below the 10th 
percentile in the climatology and at least for Burlington, it 
could be the coolest daytime high for the date since at least 
1990. We'll have very dry low level air ahead of this system, so
upon saturation temperatures will tend to steady or even fall 
during the day as rain spreads northeastward through the region.
Timing of rain looks fairly consistent with onset during the 
morning, mostly in northern New York through 10 AM and by noon 
into western portions of Vermont. A later onset timing would 
allow for high temperatures to occur relatively early in the day
before rain arrives. Duration of rain for any given location 
looks largely 6 to 12 hours, so for most places much of the 
daytime hours look wet. The intensity of rain will vary from 
light to moderate. Some of the highest rainfall rates could be 
near 0.3"/hour, but mostly in the 0.02" to 0.08"/hour rate. As 
such, total rainfall largely looks like somewhere in the 0.3" to
0.6" range, with the higher amounts favored over the 
Adirondacks and eastward into south central Vermont. 

Conditions look moderately breezy, especially through midday Sunday, 
which will result in wind chills in the higher terrain dropping into 
the 30s. As such, anyone out in the mountains should consider cool 
weather rain gear. Wind fields won't be overly strong, given modest 
gradient flow, with 25 to 30 MPH southerly low level flow 
anticipated. Rain stabilized air will limit mixing, although breezy 
conditions in the eastern side of the northern Champlain Valley can 
be expected due to local terrain effects. 

Following the departure of this system Sunday evening to the east, 
we'll gradually get back under a Canadian air mass as a
strengthening high pressure area builds southeastward amidst a 
large upper level ridge. Relatively weak advection and moist 
surface conditions following the rain will probably lead to fog 
early Monday morning. Aside from any early day shallow clouds, 
Monday will probably be mainly sunny under the influence of the 
large ridge. Temperatures will mostly trend a few degrees warmer
from Monday to Tuesday with conditions remaining dry. However, 
cool northeasterly flow on Tuesday will limit the moderation, 
especially if mid-level clouds associated with a wave of low 
pressure passing well south of our region make it this far 
north.

KEY MESSAGE 2: A Rex block will be in place by mid week next week, with 
high pressure centered to our north while low pressure develops off 
the Mid Atlantic. While the weather will be pleasant, temperatures 
will likely remain below normal, with highs in the 50s/low 60s in 
spite of sunshine. Clear skies and light winds will allow for chilly 
overnights, and patchy frost will be possible in the 
Adirondacks/eastern VT valleys each morning. Things become less 
certain from Thursday onward as there are significant differences in 
model solutions in how quickly the block breaks down, and if the Mid 
Atlantic troughiness and associated precipitation can lift north 
into our region. The 19/00z GFS in particular is quite pessimistic, 
lifting a broad area of rain into our area later Thursday. Low 
pressure trundles very slowly off the southern New England coast 
Friday into Saturday, and moisture wrapping back into NY/northern 
New England would not only keep widespread rain, it would also make 
for fairly chilly daytime temperatures potentially in the 40s and 
50s. It should be noted that this is one of the most extreme 
solutions and is generally not supported by the GFS ensemble 
members. The latest ECMWF and Canadian solutions likewise keep the 
high pressure and dry weather over our region for at least 24 hours 
beyond the GFS. Have stayed with the NBM/WPC forecast for Wednesday
